# 1. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
Mission 1: The AI Spotter

**Challenge:** Social media feeds, customer-support chats and weather forecasts all use AI. Can you spot where AI is at work, and explain why one source compares it to electricity and the internet?
## 1.1 Defining AI and its Purpose
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a foundational technology that is supercharging other scientific fields and, like electricity and the internet, has the potential to transform societies, economies, and politics worldwide.

Source: https://setr.stanford.edu/technology/artificial-intelligence/2026 Authors: Co-chairs Condoleezza Rice, Jennifer Widom, and Amy Zegart. Director and Editor in Chief Herbert S. Lin. Managing Editor Martin Giles.

**Key ideas:**

- AI is a **foundational technology**: other scientific fields are being boosted by it.

- The source compares it to **electricity and the internet**.

- It has the potential to transform **societies, economies and politics** worldwide.

## 1.2 The Societal and Economic Impact of AI
The real-world potential of AI is immense. Applications of AI include diagnosing diseases, personalizing social media feeds, executing sophisticated data analyses for weather modeling and powering the chatbots that handle our customer support requests. AI-powered robots can even assemble cars and minimize radiation from wildfires.

Chrystal R. China, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/artificial-intelligence-advantages-disadvantages

**Common misconception:** “AI is just robots and chatbots.” Not true. The applications named above range from diagnosing diseases to weather modeling; chatbots and robots are only two of them.

**Link to Chapter 5.4:** automation can also have significant job loss implications for the workforce.

# 2. The 5-Step Process: How AI Works
Mission 2: The Pass-or-Fail Machine

**Challenge:** A machine has to decide “pass” or “fail” for every item it sees, and it gets some wrong. Can you walk it through the five steps, then help it fix its mistakes?

Below, we’ll go through five steps that illustrate how AI works: inputs, processing, outcomes, adjustments, and assessments.
## 2.1 Input: Data Collection & Categorization
Data is first collected from various sources in the form of text, audio, video, and more. It is sorted into categories, such as those that can be read by the algorithms and those that cannot. You would then create the protocol and criteria for which data will be processed and used for specific outcomes.
## 2.2 Processing: Pattern Recognition & Sorting
Once data is gathered and input, the next step is to allow AI to decide what to do with the data. The AI sorts and deciphers the data using patterns it has been programmed to learn until it recognizes similar patterns in the data that is being filtered into the system.
## 2.3 Outcomes: Predictions & Decision Making
After the processing step, the AI can use those complex patterns to predict outcomes in customer behavior and market trends. In this step, the AI is programmed to decide whether specific data is a “pass” or “fail”—in other words, does it match previous patterns? That determines outcomes that can be used to make decisions.
## 2.4 Adjustments: Learning from Failures
When data sets are considered a “fail,” AI learns from that mistake, and the process is repeated again under different conditions. It may be that the algorithm’s rules must be adjusted to suit the data set in question or that the algorithm needs slight alteration. In this step, you might return to the outcomes step to better align with the current data set’s conditions.
## 2.5 Assessments: Synthesizing Insights & Feedback Loops
The final step for AI to complete an assigned task is assessment. Here, the AI technology synthesizes insights gained from the data set to make predictions based on the outcomes and adjustments. Feedback generated from the adjustments can be incorporated into the algorithm before moving forward.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. The 5-step process of how AI works

Coursera Staff, 2026 Source: https://www.coursera.org/articles/how-does-ai-work

**Common misconception:** “AI gets everything right the first time.” Not true. The process has an Adjustments step because some data is a “fail” and the algorithm’s rules may need to change (Section 2.4).

**Link to Chapter 7.2:** in a neural network, adjusting means changing the weights (you try this by hand in Activity 7A).
## Activity 2A: Sort the Fruit (paper activity)


| **Goal** | Walk one tiny example through all five steps, including a “fail” and an adjustment. |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | Paper and a pen. About 15 minutes. |
| **Task** | See below. |
| **Observation** | Write your rule, the pass or fail result for each item, and the number correct in each round. |
| **Reflection** | Which step caught the mistakes? Did your adjustment create any new mistake? |
| **Feedback** | Answer box. |
**Setup.** A toy “algorithm” must decide whether each item is an **apple**. It can only read two columns: **colour** and **shape**. It cannot read the smell.

**Known examples** (what the algorithm has seen before):

| **Example** | **Colour** | **Shape** | **Apple?** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K1 | red | round | yes |
| K2 | red | round | yes |
| K3 | yellow | long | no |
**Step 1, Input.** Look at the table of new items below. Cross out any column the toy algorithm cannot read.

**Step 2, Processing.** From K1 to K3, write the pattern for “apple” as one rule.

**Step 3, Outcomes.** Apply your rule to N1 to N6. Write **pass** (matches the pattern) or **fail**, then check against the “Really an apple?” column.

| **Item** | **Colour** | **Shape** | **Smell** | **Really an apple?** | **Round 1: pass or fail** | **Correct?** | **Round 2: pass or fail** | **Correct?** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N1 | red | round | sweet | yes | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| N2 | yellow | long | sweet | no | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| N3 | green | round | sweet | yes | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| N4 | red | long | spicy | no | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| N5 | green | round | sweet | yes | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| N6 | orange | round | citrus | no | ? | ? | ? | ? |
**Step 4, Adjustments.** Look at the wrong results. Change your rule to fix them, then fill in the Round 2 columns.

**Step 5, Assessments.** Count the correct answers in each round. Did the adjustment cause a new mistake? If it did, go back to Outcomes and adjust again, as Section 2.4 describes.

**Feedback box**

- Step 1: the smell column cannot be read, so cross it out (Section 2.1 says data is sorted into what algorithms can read and what they cannot).

- Step 2: “red and round means apple”.

- Round 1 (rule: red and round): N1 pass (correct), N2 fail (correct), N3 fail (**wrong**, a green apple), N4 fail (correct), N5 fail (**wrong**), N6 fail (correct). Score: 4 out of 6.

- Step 4: drop the colour requirement, so the rule becomes “round means apple”. Round 2: N1 pass (correct), N2 fail (correct), N3 pass (correct), N4 fail (correct), N5 pass (correct), N6 pass (**wrong**, an orange). Score: 5 out of 6.

- Step 5: the score improved, but the adjustment created a new mistake, so the loop goes round again. A rule such as “round, and red or green” gets all six right. That only fits these six items; new items could break it again, which is why assessment keeps feeding back into adjustments.

- Limit: real AI learns patterns from large amounts of data (Section 5.2) rather than from a rule you write by hand. This is a simplified model of the five steps.

**Quick check:** Which two steps form a loop, and why? (Hint: look back at Section 2.4.)

# 3. Types of AI (Based on Capabilities)
Mission 3: Name That AI

**Challenge:** A friend says, “I use an AI that can do anything a human can.” Which of the three types of AI is that, and does it exist today?
## 3.1 Artificial Narrow AI (Weak AI) – Present-day Applications
Artificial Narrow Intelligence, also known as Weak AI (what we refer to as Narrow AI), is the only type of AI that exists today. Any other form of AI is theoretical. It can be trained to perform a single or narrow task, often far faster and better than a human mind can.

However, it can’t perform outside of its defined task. Instead, it targets a single subset of cognitive abilities and advances in that spectrum. Siri, Amazon’s Alexa and IBM Watson® are examples of Narrow AI. Even OpenAI’s ChatGPT is considered a form of Narrow AI because it’s limited to the single task of text-based chat.

IBM Data and AI Team, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types
## 3.2 Artificial General AI (Strong AI) – Theoretical Concepts
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), also known as Strong AI, is today nothing more than a theoretical concept. AGI can use previous learnings and skills to accomplish new tasks in a different context without the need for human beings to train the underlying models. This ability allows AGI to learn and perform any intellectual task that a human being can.

IBM Data and AI Team, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types
## 3.3 Super AI – Beyond Human Cognition
Super AI is commonly referred to as artificial superintelligence and, like AGI, is strictly theoretical. If ever realized, Super AI would think, reason, learn, make judgements and possess cognitive abilities that surpass those of human beings.

The applications possessing Super AI capabilities will have evolved beyond the point of understanding human sentiments and experiences to feel emotions, have needs and possess beliefs and desires of their own.

IBM Data and AI Team, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types

| **Level** | **Capability** | **Status** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Super AI** | Surpasses humans | Theoretical |
| **General AI (AGI)** | Any human intellectual task | Theoretical |
| **Narrow AI** | One task: Siri, Alexa, ChatGPT | Exists today |
Figure 2. The three kinds of AI based on capabilities

IBM Data and AI Team, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types

**Common misconception:** “Siri and ChatGPT seem so smart that they must be general AI.” Not true. The source classes Siri, Alexa, IBM Watson and ChatGPT as Narrow AI, because each is limited to a defined task.

**Link to Chapter 4:** the practical applications there (computer vision, robotics, expert systems) all use Narrow AI.

# 4. Practical Applications & Technologies
Mission 4: The Smart Warehouse

**Challenge:** A warehouse wants machines that can see what is around them, move and sort goods, and spot trends in its data. Which kind of Narrow AI would do each job?
## 4.1 Computer Vision: Object Detection & Self-Driving Vehicles
Narrow AI applications with computer vision can be trained to interpret and analyze the visual world. This allows intelligent machines to identify and classify objects within images and video footage.

Applications of computer vision include:

- Image recognition and classification

- Object detection

- Object tracking

- Facial recognition

- Content-based image retrieval

Computer vision is critical for use cases that involve AI machines interacting and traversing the physical world around them. Examples include self-driving cars and machines navigating warehouses and other environments.
## 4.2 Robotics: Industrial Automation & Healthcare Assistance
Robots in industrial settings can use Narrow AI to perform routine, repetitive tasks that involve materials handling, assembly and quality inspections. In healthcare, robots equipped with Narrow AI can assist surgeons in monitoring vitals and detecting potential issues during procedures.

Agricultural machines can engage in autonomous pruning, moving, thinning, seeding and spraying. And smart home devices such as the iRobot Roomba can navigate a home’s interior using computer vision and use data stored in memory to understand its progress.
## 4.3 Expert Systems: Data Trends & Complex Problem Solving
Expert systems equipped with Narrow AI capabilities can be trained on a corpus to emulate the human decision-making process and apply expertise to solve complex problems. These systems can evaluate vast amounts of data to uncover trends and patterns to make decisions. They can also help businesses predict future events and understand why past events occurred.

IBM Data and AI Team, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types

Figure 3. Practical applications of Narrow AI

**Common misconception:** “A robot that does many jobs must be general AI.” Not true. The robots described here use Narrow AI for routine, defined tasks, and Section 3.1 says Narrow AI cannot perform outside its defined task.

# 5. AI vs. Traditional Programming: Advantages & Disadvantages
Mission 5: The Tool Picker

**Challenge:** A company has two projects: a rule checker where every decision must be traceable, and a tagger for thousands of photos and videos. Should each one use traditional programming or AI?

As with any technology, there are advantages and disadvantages of AI, when compared to traditional programming technologies. Aside from foundational differences in how they function, AI and traditional programming also differ significantly in terms of programmer control, data handling, scalability and availability.

| **Traditional** | **AI** |
| --- | --- |
| Control: Full, traceable logic | Control: Black box, hard to explain |
| Data: Structured only | Data: Images, video, text |
| Learning: Manual updates | Learning: Learns from new data |
| Stability: Same result every time | Stability: May be inconsistent |
| Scalability: Needs more code | Scalability: Scales quickly |
| 24/7 use: Often needs staff | 24/7 use: Runs unattended |
Figure 4. AI vs. traditional programming at a glance
## 5.1 Control and Transparency (The “Black Box” Problem)
Traditional programming offers developers full control over the logic and behavior of software, allowing for precise customization and predictable, consistent outcomes. And if a program doesn’t behave as expected, developers can trace back through the codebase to identify and correct the issue.

AI systems, particularly complex models like deep neural networks, can be hard to control and interpret. They often work like “black boxes,” where the input and output are known, but the process the model uses to get from one to the other is unclear. This lack of transparency can be problematic in industries that prioritize process and decision-making explainability (like healthcare and finance).
## 5.2 Learning Capability & Unstructured Data Handling
Traditional programming is rigid; it relies on structured data to execute programs and typically struggles to process unstructured data. In order to “teach” a program new information, the programmer must manually add new data or adjust processes. Traditionally coded programs also struggle with independent iteration. In other words, they may not be able to accommodate unforeseen scenarios without explicit programming for those cases.

Because AI systems learn from vast amounts of data, they’re better suited for processing unstructured data like images, videos and natural language text. AI systems can also learn continually from new data and experiences (as in machine learning), allowing them to improve their performance over time and making them especially useful in dynamic environments where the best possible solution can evolve over time.
## 5.3 Stability vs. Scalability
Traditional programming is stable. Once a program is written and debugged, it will perform operations the exact same way, every single time. However, the stability of rules-based programs comes at the expense of scalability. Because traditional programs can only learn through explicit programming interventions, they require programmers to write code at scale in order to scale up operations. This process can prove unmanageable, if not impossible, for many organizations.

AI programs offer more scalability than traditional programs but with less stability. The automation and continuous learning features of AI-based programs enable developers to scale processes quickly and with relative ease, representing one of the key advantages of AI. However, the improvisational nature of AI systems means that programs may not always provide consistent, appropriate responses.
## 5.4 Efficiency, 24/7 Availability, and Workforce Implications
Rules-based computer programs can provide 24/7 availability, but sometimes only if they have human workers to operate them around the clock.

AI technologies can run 24/7 without human intervention so that business operations can run continuously. Another of the benefits of artificial intelligence is that AI systems can automate boring or repetitive jobs (like data entry), freeing up employees’ bandwidth for higher-value work tasks and lowering the company’s payroll costs.

It’s worth mentioning, however, that automation can have significant job loss implications for the workforce. For instance, some companies have transitioned to using digital assistants to triage employee reports, instead of delegating such tasks to a human resources department. Organizations will need to find ways to incorporate their existing workforce into new workflows enabled by productivity gains from the incorporation of AI into operations.

Chrystal R. China, 2024 Source: https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/artificial-intelligence-advantages-disadvantages

**Common misconception:** “AI is always better than traditional programming.” Not true. Traditional programming gives full control and the same result every time; AI scales quickly and handles images, video and text. Each wins on different rows of Figure 4.

**Link to Chapter 7.3:** the symbolic vs connectionist table shows the same explainability trade-off.

| **Feedback** | Answer box. |
**Setup.** For each requirement, write **traditional** or **AI**, and name the row of Figure 4 (control, data, learning, stability, scalability or 24/7 use) that decided it.

| **#** | **Requirement** | **Traditional or AI?** | **Deciding row** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Every decision must be traceable back through the logic (as in healthcare or finance). | ? | ? |
| 2 | Sort a large collection of photos and videos by what they show. | ? | ? |
| 3 | The program must give the exact same result every single time. | ? | ? |
| 4 | Operations must scale up quickly without writing code at scale. | ? | ? |
| 5 | The system must run around the clock without staff operating it. | ? | ? |
| 6 | The program must improve as new data arrives and the best solution changes. | ? | ? |
**Feedback box**

- 1 = traditional (control: full, traceable logic; Section 5.1 says AI’s black-box nature is a problem where explainability matters).

- 2 = AI (data: images, video, text; Section 5.2).

- 3 = traditional (stability: same result every time; Section 5.3).

- 4 = AI (scalability: scales quickly; Section 5.3).

- 5 = AI (24/7 use: runs unattended; Section 5.4).

- 6 = AI (learning: learns from new data; Section 5.2).

- Reflection: if a requirement matched both columns (for example, scale and traceability), you would be trading one advantage for another.

- Limit: this activity only uses the six rows of Figure 4. Real projects involve many more factors.

**Quick check:** Section 5.4 lists a workforce risk of AI automation. What is it, and what example does the section give?

# Where Chapters 6–8 fit
Chapters 1–5 told you *what AI is*. The next three chapters answer a deeper question: **how do you actually build something that behaves intelligently?** There are three big answers, and each one makes a different bet.

| **Approach** | **The bet** | **One-line summary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Symbolic AI** (Ch. 6) | Intelligence is **reasoning with rules** | Humans write the knowledge down; the machine reasons with it |
| **Connectionist AI** (Ch. 7) | Intelligence is **patterns learned from data** | A network of simple units adjusts itself from examples |
| **Behaviourist AI** (Ch. 8) | Intelligence is **acting well in the world** | Simple behaviours, or rewards, shape what the agent does |
Figure 5. Three approaches to building AI

**Prerequisites:** Chapters 1–3 (what AI is, the 5-step process, types of AI). No coding experience needed.

**Suggested route:** read the chapter intro, do the activity *before* reading the explanation if you can, then check your result against the Feedback box.
# 6. Symbolic AI: Reasoning with Rules
Mission 6: The Rulebook Detective

**Challenge:** A clinic wants a program that flags possible pneumonia from a patient’s symptoms. No training data is available. Could you build it by writing down what doctors know?
## 6.1 What is Symbolic AI?
Symbolic AI represents knowledge using **symbols**: names for objects and concepts, plus relationships between them. It then reasons by applying logical **rules** to those symbols (DataCamp, 2023). Instead of learning from huge piles of data, a human *writes the knowledge down*.

A classic example is a medical rule of the form:

IF the patient has a fever AND a cough AND difficulty breathing, THEN the patient may have pneumonia.

The system checks the facts about a patient against its rules and draws a conclusion. A collection of facts and rules like this is called a **knowledge base**, and a program built on one that gives advice in a specialist area is an **expert system**.
## 6.2 Strengths and limits


| **Strength** | **Why** |
| --- | --- |
| **Explainable** | You can trace a conclusion back to the exact rules used |
| **Easy to edit** | Change a rule and the behaviour changes |
| **Needs little data** | The knowledge is written by people, not learned from examples |


| **Limit** | **Why** |
| --- | --- |
| **Needs well-defined knowledge** | If the rules are incomplete, the system can fail |
| **Hard to scale** | More symbols and rules can make reasoning very expensive |
| **Poor with uncertainty** | It prefers precise, unambiguous facts |
| **Limited learning** | It usually must be reprogrammed by hand |
**Common misconception:** “Symbolic AI is old, so it’s useless.” Not true. Rule-based reasoning is still used where explanations matter, and symbolic and learning-based methods can be **combined** into hybrid systems (DataCamp, 2023).

**Link to Chapter 4.3:** the expert systems you met earlier are a form of symbolic AI.
## Activity 6A: Build a Family Detective (SWISH / Prolog)


| **Goal** | See how conclusions follow from facts and rules, and practise stating relationships precisely. |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | A browser. Open **SWISH** (SWI-Prolog online) at swish.swi-prolog.org and start a new program. SWISH’s documentation says it does not require a login by default and only runs safe commands, so no account should be needed. Open it once on your own network before the activity, in case it is blocked. |
| **Task** | See below. |
| **Observation** | Write down each query, your *prediction*, and the actual answer. |
| **Reflection** | Which results surprised you? What does that tell you about the rules you wrote? |
| **Feedback** | Compare with the answer box. |
**Syntax in 30 seconds:** `parent(alice, bob).` is a **fact** (“alice is a parent of bob”). Names starting with a lowercase letter are specific things. Uppercase names like `X` are **variables** that Prolog fills in. `:-` means “is true if”, and a comma means “and”. Every statement ends with a full stop.

**Step 1.** Type this knowledge base into the program window:

`parent(tom, alice).`

`parent(alice, bob).`

`parent(alice, carol).`

`parent(bob, dave).`

` `

`grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).`

`sibling(X, Y) :- parent(P, X), parent(P, Y), X \= Y.`

**Step 2. Predict, then query.** Before running each query in the query box, write your prediction.

1. `?- grandparent(tom, X).`

2. `?- grandparent(alice, X).`

3. `?- sibling(bob, X).`

4. `?- sibling(dave, X).`

**Step 3. Extend it.** Add this rule and predict `?- auntOrUncle(carol, X).` before running it:

`auntOrUncle(X, Y) :- sibling(X, P), parent(P, Y).`

**Step 4. Break it on purpose.** Delete `, X \= Y` from the `sibling` rule and run `?- sibling(bob, X).` again. What changed, and why?

**Feedback box**

- Query 1 gives `X = bob` and `X = carol` (tom’s child alice has children bob and carol).

- Query 2 gives `X = dave`.

- Query 3 gives `X = carol`.

- Query 4 gives `false`: dave’s parent bob has no other children.

- `auntOrUncle(carol, X)` gives `X = dave`: carol’s sibling is bob, and bob’s child is dave.

- Without `X \= Y`, bob counts as his own sibling, because both “bob” slots can match the same child of alice. The rule was *logically valid but incomplete*: it did not say what we obviously assumed. Symbolic AI only knows what you tell it.

**Stretch (computational thinking):** write facts for a toy symptom checker (`symptom(patient1, fever).` and so on) and a rule `may_have_pneumonia(P)` that needs three symptoms. This is a teaching toy, not medical advice.

**Quick check:** Why can you *explain* any answer this program gives, but not always explain a neural network’s answer? (Hint: look back at Section 5.1.)

# 7. Connectionist AI: Learning from Data
Mission 7: The Canteen Neuron

**Challenge:** Nobody can write rules for “what does a cat look like in a photo?” What if a program could *learn* the rules by adjusting itself from examples?
## 7.1 What is connectionism?
**Connectionism** explains intelligent behaviour using **artificial neural networks** (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). A network is made of many simple **units** (loosely inspired by brain cells) joined by connections. Each connection has a **weight** that says how strongly one unit influences another. Weights can be positive or negative.

Units are usually grouped into three kinds:

- **Input units** receive the information to be processed.

- **Hidden units** sit in between and pass signals along.

- **Output units** hold the result.

Each unit works out its own activation from the signals it receives, then passes it on. **The knowledge of the network lives in its weights.**
## 7.2 How does it learn?
Finding good weights is the central goal. Learning methods such as **backpropagation** calculate adjustments to the weights so the network does better on its training examples. Training often takes a huge number of rounds of adjustment (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy).

**Misconception check:** artificial neural networks are *inspired by* the brain but are **much simpler** than real brains. “Neuron” here means a small calculation, not a living cell.
## 7.3 Symbolic vs connectionist


|  | **Symbolic** | **Connectionist** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge comes from | Humans writing rules | Patterns learned from data |
| Explains its answers? | Usually yes | Often hard (the “black box”, Section 5.1) |
| Needs lots of data? | No | Usually yes |
| Good at | Logic, structured knowledge | Perception, such as images |
## 7.4 Types of neural networks (your mind map)
Your mind map lists feedforward, convolutional (CNN), recurrent (RNN) and Transformer networks. One beginner-friendly sentence on each:

- **Feedforward:** information moves in one direction, from the input units through the hidden units to the output units, so each layer’s output becomes the next layer’s input (IBM, “What is a neural network?”).

- **Convolutional (CNN):** similar to a feedforward network, but usually used for image recognition, pattern recognition and computer vision (IBM, “What is a neural network?”). The CNN Explainer (Wang et al., 2020) is an interactive tool designed for beginners.

- **Recurrent (RNN):** a deep neural network trained on sequential or time series data, so it can make predictions from sequences (IBM, “What is a recurrent neural network?”).

- **Transformer:** a neural network architecture for sequential data, best known from large language models, built around a self-attention mechanism that picks out relationships between parts of an input (IBM, “What is a transformer model?”).

## Activity 7A: Be the Neuron (paper activity)


| **Goal** | Understand that a unit combines weighted inputs, and that *learning means changing weights*. |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | Paper and a pen. |
| **Task** | See below. |
| **Observation** | Fill in the output for each case, before and after the weight change. |
| **Reflection** | Which weight change made the unit more or less willing to “go”? |
| **Feedback** | Answer box. |
**Setup.** A neuron decides “Go to the canteen?” (1 = go, 0 = stay). It adds up weighted inputs and goes if the **total is 2 or more**.

| **Input** | **Meaning** | **Weight** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Friend going (1 or 0) | A friend is going | **+2** |
| Raining (1 or 0) | It is raining | **-3** |
| Hungry (1 or 0) | You are hungry | **+2** |
**Part 1.** Work out the total and decision for each case.

| **Case** | **Friend** | **Rain** | **Hungry** | **Total** | **Go?** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1 | 0 | 0 | ? | ? |
| B | 1 | 1 | 0 | ? | ? |
| C | 0 | 1 | 1 | ? | ? |
| D | 0 | 0 | 1 | ? | ? |
| E | 1 | 1 | 1 | ? | ? |
**Part 2.** “Train” the neuron: change the Rain weight from -3 to **-1**. Recalculate cases B, C and E.

**Feedback box**

- Part 1: A = 2, go. B = -1, stay. C = -1, stay. D = 2, go. E = 1, stay.

- Part 2 (rain weight -1): B = 1, stay. C = 1, stay. E = 3, **go**. Only case E changed.

- Lesson: no rule was rewritten. Only a number changed, and behaviour changed with it. Real networks do the same with huge numbers of weights, adjusted automatically by learning algorithms.

- Limit of this analogy: a real network learns its weights from many examples; you set them by hand here.

## Activity 7B: Playground Lab (TensorFlow Playground)


| **Goal** | Predict and observe how network settings change learning. |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | Open TensorFlow Playground (playground.tensorflow.org) in a browser. Note the date you used it, since the controls may change. |
| **Task** | Pick one dataset. Predict whether a network with **no hidden layer** can separate it. Run it. Then add one hidden layer and compare. Change **one setting at a time** (for example learning rate, or number of neurons). |
| **Observation** | For each run, record the setting you changed, the training loss and the test loss, and whether the shape of the boundary changed. |
| **Reflection** | Which change helped most? Did any change make test loss worse than training loss? |
| **Feedback** | Expected outcomes below. |
**Feedback box**

- With no hidden layer and only the raw x and y inputs, the network can only draw a straight-line boundary. Expect it to separate data that a straight line can split, and to struggle with the circle, exclusive-or and spiral datasets.

- Adding a hidden layer with a few neurons lets the boundary bend, so the circle and exclusive-or datasets usually become separable. The spiral is the hardest and usually needs more neurons or more layers.

- A very high learning rate can make the loss jump around instead of settling; a very low one learns slowly. More neurons help up to a point.

- If the test loss ends up much higher than the training loss, the network may be fitting the training points too closely.

- These are the usual behaviours of this tool, written from general knowledge of how it works rather than from your exact settings, so treat them as predictions to test against your own runs.

**Fallback if the site is unavailable:** include 2–3 screenshots of runs and ask learners to explain the difference between them.

# 8. Behaviourist AI: Acting and Learning from Rewards
Mission 8: The Confused Vacuum

**Challenge:** A robot vacuum must avoid furniture, return to its dock, and still clean the floor. Do you need a giant world model, or can simple behaviours stacked together do the job?

**Two ideas, one chapter.** (1) **Behaviour-based AI** builds intelligent action from layered simple behaviours. (2) **Reinforcement learning** learns good actions from rewards. They are different techniques; both focus on *behaviour* rather than on written rules or stored knowledge.
## 8.1 Behaviour-based AI
By the 1980s, researchers found it hard to use symbolic AI in real robots. This led to a “reactive” approach: low-level behaviours that respond to the world directly, without building a detailed internal model first. Rodney Brooks introduced the **subsumption architecture** for this (Moore, 2016).

- A subsumption architecture is a **hierarchy of simple behaviours** (Wooldridge, Parsons and Payne, course slides).

- Each behaviour is a rather simple, rule-like structure, and complex behaviour **emerges** from simple components interacting with the environment (same slides).

- Higher layers can take over (subsume) lower ones when appropriate (University of York Brooks page).

Brooks later founded iRobot, the company behind the Roomba robot vacuum, but the subsumption approach has been criticised as hard to scale to more complex robots (Moore, 2016).

**Misconception check:** “Behaviour-based means no rules.” Not quite. The behaviours are simple rules; the difference is that there is no large symbolic model of the world.
## Activity 8A: Layer the Vacuum (paper activity)


| **Goal** | See how priority layers of simple behaviours produce sensible action. |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | Paper and a pen. |
| **Task** | A toy robot has three behaviours, ranked from **highest to lowest priority**: (1) **Avoid**: if the bumper is pressed, turn away. (2) **Dock**: if the battery is low, head to the charger. (3) **Wander**: otherwise, move forward. For each situation, decide which behaviour takes control. |
| **Observation** | Fill in the table. |
| **Reflection** | What happens if you swap the priority of Avoid and Dock? |
| **Feedback** | Answer box. |


| **Situation** | **Bumper pressed?** | **Battery low?** | **Which behaviour wins?** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | No | No | ? |
| 2 | No | Yes | ? |
| 3 | Yes | No | ? |
| 4 | Yes | Yes | ? |
**Feedback box**

- 1 = Wander. 2 = Dock. 3 = Avoid. 4 = Avoid (highest priority wins).

- Swapping priorities: in situation 4 the robot would drive toward the charger *into* the obstacle. Priority order is a design decision, and wrong priorities cause bad behaviour.

- Limit: this is a **simplified teaching model** inspired by subsumption, not a description of how any real vacuum works.

## 8.2 Reinforcement learning
In **reinforcement learning (RL)**, an **agent** learns by interacting with an **environment**. It takes an action, the environment responds with a new situation and a **reward** (or penalty), and the agent adjusts to earn more reward over time. The strategy it learns is called a **policy**. Unlike supervised learning, RL does not rely on labelled examples; it learns by **trial and error** (OVHcloud; Verpex).

Two ideas to remember:

- **Exploration vs exploitation:** try new things, or repeat what already worked?

- **Delayed rewards:** some actions pay off only later, which makes learning harder.

**Link to the guide:** the “Adjustments” step in Chapter 2 is a loose picture of feedback improving behaviour. RL is one concrete way that happens.
## Activity 8B: Three Doors (dice game, exploration vs exploitation)


| **Goal** | Feel the exploration/exploitation trade-off. |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparation** | One die per pair, paper, 10 minutes. |
| **Task** | You are an agent choosing among 3 doors for 15 rounds. **Rules (hidden from the player; the partner reads them):** Door A always pays +1. Door B pays +5 if the die shows 6, otherwise 0. Door C pays +3 if the die shows 4, 5 or 6, otherwise 0. The player picks a door, the partner rolls (if needed) and announces the reward. Keep a tally. |
| **Observation** | After 15 rounds record total reward, how many times you tried each door, and when you decided which door was best. |
| **Reflection** | Did you stop exploring too early? What would a better strategy be? |
| **Feedback** | Answer box. |
**Feedback box**

- Average reward per round: A = 1; B = 5 x 1/6, about 0.83; C = 3 x 1/2 = 1.5. So **C is best on average**.

- Over only a few rounds luck can mislead you: B might pay +5 on the first try and look best. That is exactly why agents must keep exploring for a while before committing.

- This is a simplified RL-style game (there is only one situation, so no “state”). Full RL adds changing situations and delayed rewards.

# Glossary


| **Term** | **Meaning** |
| --- | --- |
| **Artificial intelligence (AI)** | A foundational technology with the potential to transform societies, economies and politics |
| **Narrow AI** | AI trained to perform a single or narrow task; the only type that exists today |
| **Artificial general intelligence (AGI)** | Theoretical AI that could learn and perform any intellectual task a human can |
| **Super AI** | Theoretical AI whose abilities would surpass those of human beings |
| **Computer vision** | Narrow AI trained to interpret and classify images and video |
| **Black box** | A model whose input and output are known but whose inner process is unclear |
| **Unstructured data** | Data such as images, video and natural language text |
| **Symbolic AI** | AI that reasons over symbols using human-written rules |
| **Knowledge base** | A collection of facts and rules a symbolic system reasons with |
| **Expert system** | A rule-based system that gives advice in a specialist area |
| **Connectionism** | The approach that builds AI from networks of simple connected units |
| **Weight** | A number that sets how strongly one unit influences another |
| **Backpropagation** | A learning method that adjusts weights to reduce errors |
| **Subsumption architecture** | A hierarchy of simple behaviours where higher layers can override lower ones |
| **Emergent behaviour** | Complex behaviour arising from simple parts interacting with the world |
| **Reinforcement learning** | Learning actions by trial and error using rewards and penalties |
| **Agent / Environment / Reward / Policy** | The learner / what it acts in / its feedback / its learned strategy |
